text.p: Australian average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 0.7 percent in the three months to August, to be 3.5 percent higher over the year, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said. Economists' median forecasts had been for a 1.0 percent quarterly rise and a 3.7 annual rise. A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow:
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"I think the monetary authorities will be nearly at the stage of (being) ready to push the button on interest rates. I think they are still a little bit concerned about some of these pace setting enterprise bargains, but certainly the fact the wages data today do tend to follow the cycle more closely than some of these enterprise bargains suggests that perhaps the economy is not as strong as what the Reserve Bank thought it was when it wrote its article on the economy two to three weeks ago."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"An excellent number. It looks like wage settlements do have in mind lower inflation and wage claims are far from excessive. Combined with low inflation, it's difficult to see why a rate cut cannot be given."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"I thought it would be a bit stronger. The enterprise agreements have been pretty strong. Obviously, they haven't shown up in today's weekly earnings figures and it's come in very much at the low end of expectations and I think that's an unequivocally very good result. It certainly does increase the odds on a rate cut before Christmas."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH:

"They're slightly weaker than expected. Certainly backing up from yesterday's CPI it does leave the door wide open for the Reserve Bank to cut interest rates. But the question is now whether this is sufficient to authorise a cut at the November meeting. I have a hunch they may just wait another month until they see the capital expenditure and latest round of enterprise agreements data before agreeing to an interest rate cut."

"I think this number well and truly paves the way for a cut in the December quarter. We're a bit ambivalent about November mainly because of the tactics involved. I think after the Reserve Bank has made such a fuss about enterprise bargaining being the leading indicator of wages, they'll probably want to hold off for awhile just to try and ensure that the message is getting home that enterprise bargaining outcomes have got to be less. The market has now built in a full half a percent cut in the cash rate, which I think is appropriate. In my view, it probably can't go a lot further."

"It's obviously a pleasing outcome. The degree of moderation in AWOTE would seem to indicate that enterprise agreements, even though we haven't seen the latest data on those, have moderated as well, which is something that has been a key focus for the Reserve Bank. The data obviously raises the probability of a near-term rate cut with most likely timing being after the November board meeting. There is still a question mark over whether they may hold out for a few weeks after the board meeting to see the DIR (Department of Industrial Relations) enterprise agreements data."
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH:

"A better than expected figure...I think it paves the way for a rate cut here. The Reserve Bank will particularly like the aggregate wages number which was flat. One thing to be cautious of in the data is the bureau warns that they've changed the sample ... this could have had an effect on the estimates of quarterly change and also they warn that in interpreting AWOTE a number of new enterprise agreements includes some absorption of overtime earnings into ordinary time earnings. So that would actually add upward bias I think. Because when we look at the figure for total earnings it was flat, so some earnings have been taken away from the total and put in the (AWOTE) numbers."
